notes: Real-world sub-GHz emitters a CC1101 can observe. 'detect' is how: decode = protocol decoded and checksum-verified; pulses = demodulated pulses seen, identified by band only; energy = RSSI sweep only (content not demodulated). 'role': mobile/device = a transmitter whose signal strength says how close it is; base = fixed infrastructure (tower, repeater) that only says a system is in range. eirp_dbm is a typical radiated power used for rough distance estimates. Bands follow current US (FCC) and EU/CEPT allocations.

entries.name: Public-safety radio transmitting (800 MHz NPSPAC)
entries.meaning: A police, fire or EMS radio (handheld or vehicle) is keying up. 806-809 MHz is the mobile-transmit half of the NPSPAC band, licensed only to public safety; it carries mutual-aid/interop channels (8CALL90/8TAC91-94 at 806.0125-806.5125 MHz) and many county/state trunked systems.
entries.caveats: Energy only: P25/analog/DMR content is not demodulated, so police vs fire vs EMS can't be told apart without your local frequency list (--local-freqs).

entries.name: Trunked/conventional radio transmitting (800 MHz)
entries.meaning: A handheld or vehicle radio is transmitting to an 800 MHz repeater or trunked site. Most county/city P25 systems for police, fire and EMS live here, shared with utilities, transit and business users.
entries.caveats: Shared band. Add your county's system (RadioReference) via --local-freqs to label channels exactly.

entries.name: Public-safety radio transmitting (700 MHz)
entries.meaning: A state/local public-safety radio is transmitting. 799-805 MHz is the mobile-transmit side of the 700 MHz narrowband public-safety band (paired with 769-775 MHz) and is licensed only to public-safety agencies.
entries.caveats: Energy only; agency not identifiable without --local-freqs.

entries.name: FirstNet / AT&T Band 14 LTE device transmitting
entries.meaning: An LTE device on Band 14 is transmitting: FirstNet (first-responder phones, vehicle routers in patrol cars and engines) or an ordinary AT&T customer, since AT&T carries commercial traffic on Band 14.
entries.caveats: Weak indicator of first responders on its own; strongest when it coincides with 700/800 MHz public-safety radio activity.

entries.name: 800 MHz trunked radio site (tower) in range
entries.meaning: Repeater/trunked-site transmitters. Control channels transmit continuously; voice channels light up whenever anyone on the system talks, wherever they are. Shows which systems cover you, not who is nearby.
entries.caveats: Not a proximity signal - use the 806-816 MHz mobile-transmit entries for that.

entries.name: 700 MHz public-safety site (tower) in range
entries.meaning: Base/repeater side of the 700 MHz public-safety band.
entries.caveats: Below the CC1101's specified 779 MHz limit; needs --extended-range and sensitivity is reduced.

entries.name: Emergency-services TETRA radio transmitting
entries.meaning: A police, fire or ambulance TETRA terminal (handheld or vehicle) is transmitting. 380-385 MHz is the terminal-transmit half of the harmonised European emergency-services band (BOS-Digitalfunk, Airwave, C2000, RAKEL, ASTRID...). Terminals also send short registration bursts when idle.
entries.caveats: Below the CC1101's specified 387 MHz limit; needs --extended-range. TDMA bursts are short, so a fast sweep helps.

entries.name: Emergency-services TETRA base station in range
entries.meaning: TETRA base stations of the emergency-services network. Continuous carriers; shows coverage, not proximity.

entries.name: Federal government radio transmitting (406-420 MHz)
entries.meaning: The 406.1-420 MHz band is reserved for US federal users: law enforcement (FBI, DHS/ICE/CBP, US Marshals, Secret Service), military, park rangers and other agencies.
entries.caveats: Many non-police federal users too; much of it encrypted. Energy only.

entries.name: UHF two-way radio transmitting (450-470 MHz)
entries.meaning: Conventional UHF radio: some police/fire departments, schools, security guards, construction, hospitals, retail. Repeater outputs are mostly 451-454 and 460-462 MHz, mobile inputs 456-459 and 465-467 MHz.
entries.caveats: Very mixed band; label your local agencies with --local-freqs. Above 464 MHz needs --extended-range.

entries.name: FRS/GMRS walkie-talkie
entries.meaning: Consumer walkie-talkies (FRS channels 1-22, GMRS). Common with families, events, hunters, security staff.
entries.caveats: 467 MHz channels need --extended-range.

entries.name: Freight train end-of-train device
entries.meaning: End-of-train (EOT) units on the last car report brake-line pressure to the locomotive on 452.9375 MHz (locomotive replies on 457.9375). A strong signal means a train is passing close by.

entries.name: PMR446 walkie-talkie
entries.meaning: Licence-free consumer walkie-talkies (500 mW).

entries.name: Amateur radio (70 cm band)
entries.meaning: Licensed amateur operators, repeaters and satellites. In Europe the band is 430-440 MHz.

entries.name: Paging transmitter (POCSAG/FLEX)
entries.meaning: Commercial paging networks used by hospitals, on-call staff and some fire departments. High-power towers broadcasting to pagers; bursts mean pages are going out, not that someone is near.
entries.caveats: Above the CC1101's specified 928 MHz limit; needs --extended-range.

entries.name: Cell phone / cellular modem transmitting (850 MHz)
entries.meaning: A phone, hotspot, car telematics unit or IoT modem is transmitting to a tower (LTE Bands 5/26, 5G n5). Phones transmit during calls and data use; a strong signal means the device is very close.
entries.caveats: Energy only. Lower 814-816 MHz overlaps 800 MHz land-mobile in some areas.

entries.name: Verizon Band 13 LTE device transmitting
entries.meaning: A Verizon LTE device is transmitting (Band 13 uplink, 777-787 MHz).
entries.caveats: 777-779 MHz is below the CC1101's specified range.

entries.name: Cell tower (850 MHz downlink)
entries.meaning: Cellular base stations. Always on.

entries.name: Mobile phone transmitting (LTE 800)
entries.meaning: A phone or modem is transmitting on LTE Band 20.

entries.name: Mobile phone transmitting (GSM/LTE 900)
entries.meaning: A phone, alarm communicator or modem is transmitting on GSM-900 / LTE Band 8.

entries.name: Cell tower (GSM/LTE 900 downlink)
entries.meaning: Cellular base stations. Always on.

entries.name: 900 MHz private radio / utility broadband
entries.meaning: Private land-mobile and utility private-LTE (Band 106) used by power companies, railroads and businesses. 896-901 MHz is the mobile-transmit side.
entries.caveats: 935-940 MHz needs --extended-range.

entries.name: LoRaWAN sensor or gateway (US915 sub-band 2)
entries.meaning: LoRaWAN uplinks on the channels used by The Things Network and Helium (903.9-905.3 MHz): parking, water-leak, asset trackers, smart-city sensors.
entries.caveats: LoRa chirps are not demodulated by a CC1101; detected by energy.

entries.name: Meshtastic LoRa mesh node
entries.meaning: Off-grid messaging radios on Meshtastic's default US LongFast channel (906.875 MHz).
entries.caveats: Nodes on non-default channels show up as generic 915 MHz ISM activity.

entries.name: Z-Wave smart-home device
entries.meaning: Z-Wave locks, switches, thermostats and sensors (Ring Alarm, SmartThings, Yale/Schlage locks) on 908.42 / 916 MHz.
entries.caveats: Very low power; only seen within a few tens of metres.

entries.name: Smart utility meter / 915 MHz hopping network
entries.meaning: Electric, gas and water meters (Itron ERT, Neptune R900, Landis+Gyr Gridstream, Sensus) hop across this range every few seconds. Activity on many channels at once is typical of a meter neighbourhood.
entries.caveats: Shares the ISM band with many other devices.

entries.name: 915 MHz ISM device
entries.meaning: Licence-free 902-928 MHz devices: weather stations, LoRa, Amazon Sidewalk, baby monitors, long-range drone/RC links (ExpressLRS, Crossfire), amateur 33 cm.
entries.caveats: Generic band match only.

entries.name: 868 MHz SRD device
entries.meaning: European short-range devices: Homematic, alarm sensors, LoRaWAN, Sigfox, weather stations, smart meters.
entries.caveats: Generic band match only.

entries.name: LoRaWAN sensor (EU868)
entries.meaning: LoRaWAN uplinks on the EU868 channels (867.1-868.5 MHz).
entries.caveats: Shares 868.0-868.6 with many SRDs.

entries.name: Z-Wave smart-home device
entries.meaning: Z-Wave home automation (868.42 / 869.85 MHz).

entries.name: Meshtastic LoRa mesh node
entries.meaning: Meshtastic default EU_868 channel (869.525 MHz).

entries.name: Social alarm / telecare pendant
entries.meaning: 869.200-869.250 MHz is reserved for social alarms (personal emergency buttons for elderly or disabled people).
entries.caveats: Health-related; hidden unless --allow-sensitive.

entries.name: Weather balloon (radiosonde)
entries.meaning: Radiosondes launched twice daily (00/12 UTC) by weather services transmit position and readings about once per second for ~2 hours as they climb to 30 km.
entries.caveats: US NWS sondes mostly use 1680 MHz (out of range); 400-406 MHz is used across Europe and elsewhere. Shares the band with MedRadio.

entries.name: Medical implant / body-worn device telemetry
entries.meaning: MedRadio/MICS: pacemakers, defibrillators, neurostimulators and their bedside monitors.
entries.caveats: Health-related; hidden unless --allow-sensitive. Range is only a few metres.

entries.name: Acurite temperature/humidity sensor
entries.meaning: Acurite 592TXR/06002RM tower sensor, the outdoor sensor of most Acurite home weather displays. Reports every ~16-18 s.

entries.name: LaCrosse temperature/humidity sensor
entries.meaning: LaCrosse TX141TH-Bv2 (TFA 30.3221) outdoor sensor for LaCrosse color/forecast stations. Reports every ~50 s.

entries.name: LaCrosse IT+ sensor
entries.meaning: LaCrosse/TFA TX29-IT, TX35-IT and TX25U thermometers. Report every ~4-6 s.

entries.name: Weather station outdoor array (Fine Offset WH24/WH65)
entries.meaning: The all-in-one outdoor sensor sold as Ambient Weather WS-2902, Ecowitt WS69/WS2320, Misol, Froggit and others. Wind, rain, temperature, humidity, UV, light every ~16 s.

entries.name: Ambient Weather / Ecowitt indoor-outdoor sensor
entries.meaning: WH31E / WH31B thermo-hygrometers used with Ambient Weather and Ecowitt consoles.

entries.name: Alarm system sensor (Honeywell 5800 / 2GIG, 345 MHz)
entries.meaning: Door/window contacts, motion detectors, glass-break and smoke sensors of Honeywell/Resideo/ADT and 2GIG alarm panels. They report state changes instantly and a supervision heartbeat roughly hourly.

entries.name: Alarm system sensor (Interlogix/GE/Qolsys, 319.5 MHz)
entries.meaning: Interlogix/GE/UTC Simon/Concord and Qolsys-compatible sensors transmit on 319.5 MHz.
entries.caveats: Not decoded yet; identified by frequency and timing structure.

entries.name: Fixed-code remote / sensor (EV1527/PT2262)
entries.meaning: Very common cheap encoder chip used in wireless doorbells, PIR and door sensors, remote-controlled outlets, gate/garage openers and panic buttons. Each device has a fixed 24-bit code.
entries.caveats: The chip alone doesn't say which kind of product it is. Codes are redacted by default because they can be replayed.

entries.name: Car key fob / tire-pressure sensor / garage remote (315 MHz)
entries.meaning: In North America 315 MHz carries most car key fobs, tire-pressure (TPMS) sensors on passing/parked cars, and many garage-door remotes.
entries.caveats: Identified by band and timing; specific TPMS/fob protocols are not decoded yet.

entries.name: Garage door remote (Chamberlain/LiftMaster/Genie)
entries.meaning: 310 and 390 MHz are used by Chamberlain/LiftMaster Security+ (with 315) and Genie garage openers.
entries.caveats: Rolling codes are never decoded.

entries.name: Gate/garage remote (Linear MegaCode, 318 MHz)
entries.meaning: Linear MegaCode remotes used for apartment, HOA and parking gates.

entries.name: 433.92 MHz device
entries.meaning: The busiest licence-free band: weather sensors, wireless thermometers, doorbells, remotes, TPMS (EU and some US cars), EU car key fobs, smoke alarms, pool sensors.
entries.caveats: Generic band match; no decoder matched this signal.

entries.name: Utility meter (wireless M-Bus)
entries.meaning: Water, heat, gas and electricity meters and heat-cost allocators broadcasting on 868.95 MHz (modes T1/C1). Shows manufacturer, serial and meter type; readings are usually encrypted.

rx_profiles.why: LaCrosse IT+/TFA and Fine Offset 868 MHz weather sensors
